introduction: Asked which commandment is the greatest, Jesus gives two that cannot be separated: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbour as yourself. The first reading shows what that love looks like in practice: care for the stranger, the widow, the orphan and the poor. God hears their cry. As we celebrate this Eucharist, let us open our hearts to the God who loves us first, so that his love may flow through us to others.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: God hears the cry of the poor and is gracious to all who call on him. Let us bring him our needs and the needs of the world.
intentions: For the Church: that her teaching and her works of charity may show the world that love of God and love of neighbour are one. Let us pray to the Lord.
For migrants and refugees, for widows, orphans and all who have no one to defend them: that they may find welcome, justice and friendship among us. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those burdened by debt and for those who lend: that no one may be crushed by greed, and that our economies may serve the dignity of every person. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who find it hard to love, the wounded, the bitter and the lonely: that they may experience the tenderness of God through the kindness of others. Let us pray to the Lord.
For our community: that, like the Thessalonians, we may turn from every idol and become an example of faith to those around us. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Gracious Father, you command us to love you above all things and our neighbour as ourselves. Grant what you command, and receive the prayers we make in faith. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Two commandments, one love
reflection.body:
The Law of Moses contains hundreds of commandments, and the teachers of Jesus' day loved to debate which mattered most. When a lawyer tests Jesus with this question, Jesus answers by quoting Scripture twice: the great prayer of Israel, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart," and a line from Leviticus, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." Then he ties them together: on these two hang the whole Law and the prophets.

Notice that Jesus was asked for one commandment and gave two. He will not let us choose. A love of God that ignores the neighbour becomes empty piety; a love of neighbour that forgets God slowly loses its strength and its reason. Each needs the other.

The first reading keeps us from making love vague. In Exodus, love has names: the stranger who has no rights, the widow and the orphan who have no protector, the poor man whose cloak was taken as a pledge and who will be cold tonight. God says something striking: when they cry to me, I will hear, for I am gracious. To love the neighbour is to stand where God already stands.

Paul praises the Thessalonians because they "turned to God from idols to serve a living and true God." Idols are not only statues. Anything we love more than God (money, comfort, reputation) quietly takes his place, and when that happens our love for others shrinks too. Conversion is always double: back to God, and out towards the people he puts in our path.

Love of God is not first a feeling we must produce. It is our answer to being loved: "We love him, because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19). Here at Mass we receive that love in the Word and in the Body of Christ. This week, let us choose one concrete person, perhaps a stranger, a widow or someone who cannot repay us, and let God's love for them pass through our hands.
